body: Memo of 2 Jan 2000, Marks's first widely read memo, written after reading Edward Chancellor's 'Devil Take the Hindmost'. Uses the 1720 South Sea Bubble as a template: companies financed losses by issuing stock at ever-higher prices; 'Some argued that the higher the shares rose, the more they were actually worth' - Marks's gloss: '[There's no such thing as too high a price if the concept is right...]'; the legendary company 'for carrying on an undertaking of great advantage but no one to know what it is' - gloss: '[I can't understand what it does, but that's okay]'. Isaac Newton sold early, bought back at the top and lost £20,000. RCA fell from $114 to $2.5 within three years after 1929; airlines' cumulative profit from founding to 1992 was zero despite transforming the world. Verdict quoted in his 2023 recap: 'I find the evidence of an overheated, speculative market in technology, Internet and telecommunications stocks overwhelming, as are the similarities to past manias.' Outcome (per 'Taking the Temperature', 2023): S&P 500 -46% from 2000 high to 2002 low, NASDAQ -80%. Marks's definition: a bubble is 'an irrationally elevated opinion of an asset or sector.' Markers to check: prices set on revenue or 'concept and hope'; people quitting day jobs to trade; money-losing firms funded by rising equity; transformative technology assumed to mean investor profits.
title: Marks Jan-2000 'bubble.com': the timeless markers of a mania (South Sea to TMT)

body: Cooper, Gulen and Schill, 'Asset Growth and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns' (Journal of Finance 63(4), 2008; ~1,400 citations), US 1968-2003: firms in the lowest decile of annual total-asset growth beat the highest decile by about 20% a year equal-weighted (smaller but still significant value-weighted). Asset growth beat size, B/M and momentum as a predictor, and the effect survives as the 'investment' factor (CMA) in Fama-French 5 and HXZ's q-model. Pontiff and Woodgate, 'Share Issuance and Cross-sectional Returns' (JF 2008; ~590 citations): net share issuance over the prior year predicts returns more strongly than size, B/M or momentum post-1970; buyback firms do well, issuers poorly. Loughran and Ritter, 'The New Issues Puzzle' (JF 1995; ~3,700 citations): over five years after the offer, US IPO firms returned about 5% a year and seasoned (SEO) issuers about 7%, versus 12% and 15% for size-matched non-issuers. Replicated: yes, internationally (Watanabe et al.; Titman-Wei-Xie), though CMA has been flat in the US since 2007 (our Ken French computation). Use for us: in India, QIPs, preferential allotments, warrants to promoters, rights issues and acquisition sprees after a rerating are dilution and asset-growth signals that usually come near peaks (matches our cycle-top signals). Treat a large equity raise at a high P/E as a negative base rate unless the use of cash has visible high returns.
title: Asset growth (Cooper-Gulen-Schill 2008) and net share issuance (Pontiff-Woodgate 2008; Loughran-Ritter 1995): fast balance-sheet expanders and diluters underperform
